note.text:
A material is elastic if it returns to its original shape when the force is removed (rubber, a steel spring). Plastic materials keep the new shape (clay, plasticine).
Extension = stretched length − original length.
Hooke's law: the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the load (force), provided the elastic limit is not exceeded: F = ke, where k is the spring constant (N/m or N/cm).
Beyond the elastic limit, the spring is permanently stretched and the law no longer holds.
To verify: hang loads on a spring, measure the extension for each, and plot force against extension: a straight line through the origin.

sections.heading: Elastic and plastic
sections.text:
Stretch a rubber band and let go: it returns to its original shape. Materials that do this are elastic: rubber, steel springs, the strings of a guitar.
Squeeze modelling clay: it keeps its new shape. Such materials are plastic.
Even an elastic material has a limit. Pull a spring too hard and it stays longer: you have passed its elastic limit.

sections.heading: Hooke's law
sections.text:
Robert Hooke found that, for a spring, the extension e is directly proportional to the stretching force F: double the load, double the extension.
F = ke, where k is the spring constant (stiffness), in N/m or N/cm.
Extension means the increase in length: stretched length − original length. A spring {10} cm long that stretches to {15} cm has an extension of {5} cm.

sections.heading: Checking it in the laboratory
sections.text:
• Hang the spring from a clamp next to a metre rule and read its length.
• Add loads one at a time and read the length each time.
• Work out each extension and plot load (N) against extension (cm).
Up to the limit the points lie on a straight line through the origin; after it, the line curves.

key_words.meaning: returns to its original shape when the force is removed
the largest load after which the spring still returns to its length

examples: {4} N stretches a spring {2} cm: k = {2} N/cm

mistake.why: Hooke's law is about the increase in length, not the total length.

worked_example.problem: A spring is {o} cm long. With a load of {F} N it is {n} cm long. Find the extension and the spring constant (N/cm).
steps: k = F ÷ e = {F} ÷ {n - o} = {F / (n - o)} N/cm.
worked_example.answer: e = {n - o} cm, k = {F / (n - o)} N/cm

cards.idea: Hooke's law: F = ke, as long as the elastic limit is not passed.
Beyond the elastic limit the spring does not go back to its length.
example: A spring overloaded in a game stays longer.

pick.q: A spring is loaded beyond its elastic limit, then the load is removed. What happens?
pick.r: It stays longer than its original length
w: It returns exactly to its original length
e: Only within the elastic limit does it return.
It is permanently stretched, not shortened.
pick.y: Beyond the elastic limit the deformation is permanent.

pick.q: Which material is plastic rather than elastic?
e: A steel spring springs back within its limit.
A tennis ball regains its shape.

pick.q: Hooke's law says the extension is proportional to the load…
pick.r: provided the elastic limit is not exceeded
w: only when the spring is horizontal
e: Beyond the limit the graph curves.
It applies to springs and wires too.
pick.y: The law holds only up to the limit of proportionality.

questions.prompt: A spring is {o} cm long. With a load it is {o + e} cm long. Find the extension (cm).

misconceptions.explain: That is the new length. Extension is the increase.

questions.prompt: A spring has spring constant {k} N/cm. What load gives an extension of {e} cm (N)?
A load of {F1} N stretches a spring by {e1} cm. What extension will a load of {F2} N give (cm), within the elastic limit?

misconceptions.explain: Hooke's law is about proportion: multiply by {F2} ÷ {F1}.

misconceptions.explain: That is in N/cm. Change cm to m first.
